# Tine functions, with examples

Every built-in function, with a few examples of different ways to use it. Each example is a complete piece: paste it into the DAW or a file and it plays. The same guide is in the DAW's Help tab, where the examples play in place. The short form of each function is in [REFERENCE.md](REFERENCE.md).

## Time

### fast

`fast(p, n)`: Play p n times faster (n times per bar).

`fast` squeezes a pattern so it plays several times in one bar. It is the same as `p * n`. The number can be a fraction.

The plainest use: a four-note figure played twice per bar becomes eighth notes.

```tine
voice arp = [c4 e4 g4 b4].fast(2).inst(pluck)
```

A fraction slows down as well as speeds up. Here a three-note phrase plays one and a half times per bar, so its start drifts against the bar line.

```tine
voice drums = [kick . snare . kick kick snare .]
voice line  = [e4 g4 a4].fast(3/2).inst(bell)
```

`p * n` is the same thing written as arithmetic, which reads well in a stack of parts.

```tine
voice hats = [hat . hat hat].fast(4).vel(.5)
voice kick = [kick . . .] * 2
```

It fits naturally inside [`every`](#every), for a fill on the last bar of four.

```tine
voice snare = [. snare . snare].every(4, p => p.fast(2))
```

See also: [slow](#slow), [ply](#ply), [every](#every).

### slow

`slow(p, n)`: Stretch p over n bars.

`slow` stretches a pattern over several bars. It is the opposite of [`fast`](#fast), and the same as `p / n`. Use it for long lines, chord changes and pads.

A phrase normally fills one bar. Slowed by two, each note lasts twice as long and the phrase takes two bars.

```tine
voice tune = [c4 d4 e4 g4 e4 d4 c4 .].slow(2).inst(keys)
```

Chord changes are often written as one chord per step, then slowed so each gets a bar of its own.

```tine
voice pad  = [c3@maj7 a2@m7 d3@m7 g2@7].slow(4).inst(pad)
voice beat = [kick hat snare hat]
```

A fractional slow sets up a long cycle against the bar. Five notes over three bars line up again only every three bars.

```tine
voice drone = [c2 g2 c3 bb2 f2].slow(3).inst(bass)
voice tick  = [hat*4]
```

See also: [fast](#fast), [loop](#loop), [arrange](#arrange).

### late

`late(p, t)`: Delay p by t bars: in 4/4, 1/8 is an eighth note.

`late` delays a pattern by a fraction of a bar. Short delays give offbeats and pushed rhythms; a delay of a whole step turns a pattern into its own echo.

Delay a chord by an eighth note (1/8 of a 4/4 bar) and it lands on the offbeats, the reggae skank.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 . . . g1 . . .].inst(bass)
voice skank = [c4@m . c4@m .].late(1/8).inst(keys).legato(.3)
```

A tiny delay is a feel, not a rhythm. Here the snare sits a little behind the beat.

```tine
voice kick  = [kick . kick .]
voice snare = [. snare . snare].late(1/64)
```

Layer a pattern with a late copy of itself for a canon. [`off`](#off) does this in one step.

```tine
let tune = [c4 e4 g4 e4 d4 f4 a4 f4]
voice lead   = tune.inst(pluck)
voice follow = tune.late(1/4).octave(1).inst(bell).vel(.5)
```

See also: [early](#early), [off](#off), [displace](#displace).

### early

`early(p, t)`: Shift p earlier by t bars.

`early` shifts a pattern earlier by a fraction of a bar, the mirror image of [`late`](#late). What falls off the start of the bar wraps round from the bar before.

Shift a bass line a sixteenth early and it anticipates each downbeat, a push common in funk and Latin music.

```tine
voice kick = [kick . . . kick . . .]
voice bass = [c2 . . . eb2 . f2 .].early(1/16).inst(bass)
```

Early by a whole step makes a pattern start partway through, like rotating it.

```tine
voice line = [c4 d4 e4 f4].early(1/4).inst(pluck)
```

Combined with [`late`](#late) on a second voice, a small `early` spreads two parts apart without changing their tempo.

```tine
voice left  = [c4 e4 g4 c5].early(1/96).pan(-.8).inst(keys)
voice right = [c4 e4 g4 c5].late(1/96).pan(.8).inst(keys)
```

See also: [late](#late), [rotate](#rotate).

### rev

`rev(p)`: Reverse p within each bar. On a list, reverses the list.

`rev` plays a pattern backwards within each bar. On a list it reverses the list. It is the simplest way to get a second idea out of a first.

A rising arpeggio reversed becomes a falling one.

```tine
voice up   = [c4 e4 g4 c5].inst(pluck)
voice down = [c4 e4 g4 c5].rev.octave(1).inst(bell).vel(.5)
```

Reversal keeps the rhythm's shape mirrored too: a long note at the start of the bar ends up at the end.

```tine
voice tune = [c4:3 d4 e4 g4:2].rev.inst(keys)
```

Most often it appears inside [`every`](#every), so the line turns round once in a while.

```tine
voice tune = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^5 ^6 ^5 ^3 ^2].every(4, rev).inst(pluck)
```

See also: [palindrome](#palindrome), [every](#every), [rotate](#rotate).

### every

`every(p, n, f, at: n-1)`: Apply f on one bar out of every n (the last one by default, where fills belong).

`every(n, f)` applies the function f on one bar out of every n. By default it is the last bar of each group, where fills belong. `at:` picks a different bar, counting from 0.

A drum fill: on every fourth bar, the snare part doubles up.

```tine
voice kick  = [kick . . kick . . kick .]
voice snare = [. . snare . . . snare .].every(4, p => p.fast(2))
```

Any function will do, including a named one. Here the melody turns backwards every second bar.

```tine
voice tune = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^6].every(2, rev).inst(pluck)
```

`at: 0` moves the change to the first bar of each group, so the phrase opens with the variation instead of closing with it.

```tine
voice tune = [^5 ^4 ^3 ^2].every(4, p => p.step(2), at: 0).inst(keys)
```

`every` calls can nest. The inner one fires every two bars; the outer one adds a second change every eight.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 . c2 g1].every(2, p => p.octave(1)).every(8, p => p.rev).inst(bass)
```

See also: [maybe](#maybe), [per_bar](#per_bar), [cat](#cat).

### palindrome

`palindrome(p)`: Play p forwards, then backwards, alternating bars.

`palindrome` plays a pattern forwards on one bar and backwards on the next. A phrase that goes somewhere comes back home.

A scale run up, then down.

```tine
voice run = [c4 d4 e4 f4 g4 a4 b4 c5].palindrome.inst(pluck)
```

With rhythm in the phrase, the rhythm reverses too, so long-short becomes short-long on the way back.

```tine
voice tune = [c4:3 e4 g4:2 a4:2].palindrome.inst(keys)
```

Slow it and the turn takes longer: a four-bar arch.

```tine
voice arch = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^6 ^7 ^8].palindrome.slow(2).inst(bell)
```

See also: [rev](#rev), [every](#every).

### iter

`iter(p, n)`: Rotate the start of p by 1/n each bar.

`iter(n)` starts the pattern 1/n of a bar later in itself each bar, wrapping round. After n bars it is back where it began. It is a classic way to make a short loop feel longer.

Four notes, rotated one step each bar: c e g b, then e g b c, and so on.

```tine
voice arp = [c4 e4 g4 b4].iter(4).inst(pluck)
```

On drums, iter moves the accent around the bar without changing the pattern.

```tine
voice perc = [rim . rim rim . rim . .].iter(8)
voice kick = [kick . . . kick . . .]
```

A count that does not match the phrase's length shifts it by a fraction of a step, which smears the rhythm.

```tine
voice line = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^3].iter(3).inst(bell)
```

See also: [rotate](#rotate), [early](#early).

### off

`off(p, t, f)`: Layer p with a copy shifted by t bars and transformed by f.

`off(t, f)` layers a pattern with a copy of itself moved t bars later and changed by f. It is a quick way to an echo, a harmony or a call and response.

An eighth-note offset with the copy an octave up: one line becomes a busy two-part figure.

```tine
voice arp = [c4 . e4 . g4 . e4 .].off(1/8, p => p.octave(1)).inst(pluck)
```

The copy can be any transformation. Here it is a quieter third above, so the line harmonizes itself.

```tine
voice tune = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^5].off(1/16, p => p.step(2).vel(.4)).inst(keys)
```

Leave out f and the copy is unchanged, a simple doubling in time.

```tine
voice clap = [. clap . clap].off(1/32)
```

See also: [late](#late), [echo](#echo), [stack](#stack).

### echo

`echo(p, times: 3, time: 1/8, decay: 0.6)`: Repeat each event, quieter each time.

`echo` repeats each note a few times, quieter each time. Unlike the [`delay`](#delay) effect, the repeats are real notes: they show in the piano roll, go out over MIDI and can be changed like any other.

Defaults: three repeats an eighth apart, each at 60% of the one before.

```tine
voice blip = [c5 . . . . . . .].echo.inst(bell)
```

A dotted-eighth echo (3/16 of a bar) against straight eighths gives the rolling sound of so much guitar music.

```tine
voice tune = [e4 . g4 . a4 . . .].echo(times: 4, time: 3/16, decay: .5).inst(pluck)
```

Short times and many repeats turn a hit into a ratchet that fades away.

```tine
voice snare = [. . . . . . . snare].echo(times: 6, time: 1/32, decay: .7)
```

See also: [delay](#delay), [off](#off), [ply](#ply).

### ply

`ply(p, n)`: Repeat each event n times within its own length. n may be a pattern.

`ply(n)` repeats each event n times inside its own length. The rhythm keeps its outline but every note stutters.

Each quarter note becomes two eighths.

```tine
voice line = [c4 e4 g4 e4].ply(2).inst(pluck)
```

Give `ply` a pattern to stutter only some notes. Here the last beat of the bar rolls.

```tine
voice hats = [hat hat hat hat].ply([1 1 1 3])
```

Alternate the amount bar by bar with angle brackets.

```tine
voice snare = [. snare . snare].ply(<1 2 1 4>)
```

See also: [fast](#fast), [echo](#echo), [chop](#chop).

### swing

`swing(p, amount: 1/3, div: 8)`: Delay every second subdivision (eighths by default) by a fraction of a step. 1/3 gives triplet swing (long-short 2:1), 0.2 a lighter 3:2, 0 is straight.

`swing` delays every second subdivision by part of a step. 1/3 gives triplet swing (long-short in a 2:1 ratio), smaller amounts a lighter shuffle, 0 is straight. `div` picks the subdivision: 8 for eighths, 16 for sixteenths.

Straight eighths made into a jazz swing feel.

```tine
voice ride = [ride ride ride ride ride ride ride ride].swing
voice walk = [c2 e2 g2 a2].inst(upright)
```

A lighter 0.2 for a laid-back groove that still feels mostly straight.

```tine
voice hats = [hat*8].vel([.8 .4]).swing(.2)
voice kick = [kick . . kick . . kick .]
```

`div: 16` swings sixteenths instead, the shuffle of hip hop and house.

```tine
voice hats = [hat*16].vel([.8 .4 .6 .4]).swing(.25, div: 16)
voice beat = [kick . snare .]
```

See also: [humanize](#humanize), [late](#late).

### stack

`stack(a, b, ...)`: Play patterns at the same time.

`stack` plays patterns at the same time. Curly braces do the same inside a phrase; `stack` is handy when the parts are long or already have names.

A whole drum kit as one voice.

```tine
voice drums = stack([kick . . kick . . . .], [. . snare . . . snare .], [hat*8].vel(.5))
```

Stack named parts to build a groove you can transform as a whole. Here the whole thing turns backwards every fourth bar.

```tine
let low  = [kick . kick .]
let high = [hat*8].vel(.4)
voice beat = stack(low, high).every(4, rev)
```

Stacking a line with a transposed copy of itself makes parallel harmony.

```tine
let tune = [c4 d4 e4 g4]
voice both = stack(tune, tune.transpose(7)).inst(organ)
```

See also: [cat](#cat), [seq](#seq), [union](#union).

### cat

`cat(a, b, ...)`: One pattern per bar, in turn.

`cat` plays one pattern per bar, in turn, then starts over. It is the function form of angle brackets: `cat(a, b)` is `<a b>`.

Two one-bar riffs that alternate.

```tine
voice bass = cat([c2 . c2 eb2], [f2 . g2 bb1]).inst(bass)
```

Patterns of any shape can be joined, which is useful for a groove and its fill.

```tine
let groove = [kick hat snare hat]
let fill   = [snare snare [snare snare] [tom1 tom2]]
voice drums = cat(groove, groove, groove, fill)
```

A chord progression, one chord per bar.

```tine
voice keys = cat(c4@maj7, a3@m7, d4@m7, g3@7).strum.inst(keys)
```

See also: [seq](#seq), [arrange](#arrange), [stack](#stack).

### seq

`seq(a, b, ...)`: Squeeze patterns one after another into a single bar.

`seq` squeezes several patterns one after another into a single bar. Each part gets an equal share of the bar, whatever its length.

Two two-note patterns make one four-note bar.

```tine
voice line = seq([c4 e4], [g4 c5]).inst(pluck)
```

Parts of different lengths still get equal time, so the second half here is a triplet.

```tine
voice line = seq([c4 d4], [e4 f4 g4]).inst(keys)
```

Build a bar from named fragments.

```tine
let up   = [c4 e4 g4]
let down = [g4 e4 c4]
voice arp = seq(up, down, up.octave(1), down.octave(1)).inst(bell)
```

See also: [cat](#cat), [concat](#concat).

### arrange

`arrange(p1, bars1, p2, bars2, ...)`: Chain patterns, each lasting the given number of bars, and loop the whole.

`arrange` chains patterns, each for a given number of bars, and loops the whole. It is a small form inside one voice, without sections.

Three bars of a groove, then one bar of a fill.

```tine
voice drums = arrange([kick hat snare hat], 3, [snare*4 [tom1 tom2]], 1)
```

A chord progression with uneven lengths: two bars of the tonic, one each of the others.

```tine
voice pad = arrange(c3@maj7, 2, f3@maj7, 1, g3@7, 1).inst(pad)
```

A pattern that spans several bars keeps playing through its share, so a slowed line fits naturally.

```tine
voice tune = arrange([c4 e4 g4 e4], 2, [d4 f4 a4 c5 a4 f4 d4 .].slow(2), 2).inst(keys)
```

See also: [cat](#cat), [loop](#loop).

### poly

`poly(p, steps)`: Polymeter: step through p's elements at `steps` per bar, whatever its length.

`poly(steps)` steps through a phrase at a fixed number of steps per bar, whatever its length. A three-note phrase at four steps per bar comes round on a different beat each bar: a polymeter.

Three notes at four steps per bar. The pattern lines up with the bar again every three bars.

```tine
voice three = [c4 eb4 g4].poly(4).inst(pluck)
voice kick  = [kick . . .]
```

Two polymeters against each other: five steps and seven steps over an eight-step grid.

```tine
voice a = [c4 d4 e4 g4 a4].poly(8).inst(bell)
voice b = [rim . rim . . rim .].poly(8)
```

Polymeter on a bass line keeps a short riff from settling.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 c3 bb1 g1 bb1].poly(8).inst(bass)
voice beat = [kick hat snare hat]
```

See also: [on](#on), [euclid](#euclid), [fast](#fast).

### euclid

`euclid(p, hits, steps, rot: 0)`: Spread `hits` events as evenly as possible over `steps` (Euclidean rhythm).

`euclid(hits, steps)` spreads hits as evenly as possible over steps. Many traditional rhythms come out this way: 3 over 8 is the tresillo, 5 over 8 the cinquillo. `rot:` turns the result.

Three kicks over eight steps, the tresillo.

```tine
voice kick = kick.euclid(3, 8)
voice hats = [hat*8].vel(.4)
```

Any pattern can be spread, not just a drum. Here a chord plays five times over sixteen steps.

```tine
voice stabs = c4@m7.euclid(5, 16).inst(keys).legato(.4)
```

`rot:` turns the rhythm by steps, which gives a family of related rhythms from one shape.

```tine
voice a = rim.euclid(5, 8)
voice b = clave.euclid(5, 8, rot: 2).vel(.6)
```

Odd step counts make rhythms that fit odd meters.

```tine
meter 7/8
voice clave = rim.euclid(3, 7)
voice kick  = [kick . . . . . .]
```

See also: [poly](#poly), [rhythm](#rhythm), [on](#on).

### beats

`beats(p, unit)`: Measure a phrase's steps in beats instead of dividing a bar: [c:3/2 d:1/2 e:2].beats lasts four beats. The line crosses bar lines and rests to the end of its last bar. unit is a note value (1/16) and defaults to the meter's beat.

`.beats` measures a phrase's steps in beats instead of dividing one bar. Each step is a beat unless `:` says otherwise, so `c:3/2` is a dotted quarter in 4/4. The line lasts as long as its steps add up to, crosses bar lines, and rests to the end of its last bar before it loops.

A melody written the way it is counted: dotted quarter, eighth, three triplets in two beats, and so on. It lasts three bars.

```tine
voice tune = [c4:3/2 d4:1/2 [e4 f4 g4]:2 a4:3 g4:1/2 f4:1/2 e4:4].beats.inst(keys)
```

A line that is not a whole number of bars rests until the next bar line. These five beats take two bars of 4/4, with three beats of rest.

```tine
voice call = [g4 e4 g4 a4 g4].beats.inst(pluck)
voice beat = [kick hat snare hat]
```

Give a unit to count in other note values. In sixteenths, `:3` is a dotted eighth.

```tine
voice bass = [c2:3 c2:3 c2:2 eb2:3 f2:3 g2:2].beats(1/16).inst(bass)
```

Beats follow the meter's beat unit. In 6/8 a beat is an eighth note, so these six beats fill one bar.

```tine
meter 6/8
voice jig = [d4:2 e4 f#4:2 a4].beats.inst(pluck)
```

See also: [on](#on), [slow](#slow), [rhythm](#rhythm).

### rhythm

`rhythm(p)`: The rhythm of p: its timing, lengths and settings, with each note replaced by a hit (x). Pour notes back in with on.

`.rhythm` keeps a pattern's timing and drops its pitches: every note becomes a hit. With [`notes`](#notes) and [`on`](#on), it takes a pattern apart so you can change when things happen without touching what happens.

Borrow the rhythm of a melody for a drum. The rim plays exactly when the tune does. A hit plus a pitch takes that pitch.

```tine
let tune = [c4 . e4 g4:2 . a4 g4]
voice lead = tune.inst(pluck)
voice rim  = tune.rhythm + rim
```

Take one tune's rhythm and pour another tune's notes into it.

```tine
let first  = [c4:2 e4 g4 . c5 b4 g4]
let second = [^5 ^4 ^3 ^2 ^1]
voice tune = second.on(first.rhythm).inst(keys)
```

A rhythm can be changed with the rhythm operators before the notes go back in. Here the melody's rhythm is flipped to fill its gaps.

```tine
let tune = [c4 . e4 . g4 g4 . .]
voice lead  = tune.inst(pluck)
voice reply = [e5 d5 c5].on(tune.rhythm.flip).inst(bell).vel(.5)
```

See also: [notes](#notes), [on](#on), [flip](#flip).

### notes

`notes(p, bars: 1)`: The notes of p in the order they play, without their timing, as a list. Notes that start together become a chord.

`.notes` keeps a pattern's pitches, in the order they play, and drops their timing. The result is a list, ready to be poured into a different rhythm with [`on`](#on). Notes that start together come out as one chord.

The notes of a tune, played on a new rhythm: a dotted pattern instead of even eighths.

```tine
let tune = [c4 d4 e4 g4 e4 d4 c4 .]
voice lead = tune.notes.on([x:3 x x:2 x:2]).inst(pluck)
```

[`print`](#print) shows what `notes` gives back. Chords stay together.

```tine
let comp = [c4@maj . f4@maj g4@7]
print(comp.notes)
voice keys = comp.notes.on([x . x x . x x .]).inst(keys)
```

A pattern that changes each bar needs `bars:` to collect more than one bar of notes.

```tine
let line = <[c4 e4 g4] [d4 f4 a4]>
voice lead = line.notes(bars: 2).on([x x . x x . x .]).inst(bell)
```

See also: [rhythm](#rhythm), [on](#on).

### on

`on(notes, rhythm, reset: 0)`: Play the notes one per hit of the rhythm. They loop independently, so 7 notes on a 5-hit rhythm come round together every 7 bars. In the notes, _ holds a note through the next hit and . leaves a hit silent. reset: n starts the notes again every n bars.

`notes.on(rhythm)` plays the notes one per hit. The two loop on their own, counted from the start of the section, so seven notes on a five-hit rhythm come round together every seven bars. That is how a short riff stays fresh for a long time. In the notes, `.` leaves a hit silent and `_` holds a note through the next hit.

Write a rhythm like drum tab: `x` is a hit, `X` an accent, `o` a ghost note. Three notes on that rhythm.

```tine
voice lead = [^1 ^3 ^5].on([X . . x . . X . . . x . X . . .]).inst(pluck)
```

Seven notes on a five-hit clave. The melody starts in a different place in the rhythm each bar.

```tine
let riff  = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^4 ^3 ^2 ^1]
let clave = [X . . x . . X . . . x . X . . .]
voice lead = riff.on(clave).inst(keys)
voice bass = clave + c2
```

In the notes, `.` silences a hit and `_` ties through it, so a phrase can breathe without changing the rhythm.

```tine
voice lead = [c4 e4 _ g4 . a4].on([x x x x x x x x]).inst(pluck)
```

`reset:` starts the notes again every n bars, so a long phrase lines up with a short rhythm on a schedule you choose.

```tine
voice lead = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^6 ^7].on([x . x x . x . x], reset: 2).inst(bell)
```

See also: [rhythm](#rhythm), [notes](#notes), [poly](#poly), [rotate](#rotate).

### displace

`displace(p, t)`: Move every hit t bars later, wrapping round inside the rhythm's loop.

`displace(t)` moves every hit t bars later, wrapping round inside the rhythm's loop. It keeps the rhythm and changes where it sits against the beat.

A sixteenth late: the same rhythm, now off the beat.

```tine
let r = [x . . x . . x . x . . x . . x .]
voice a = r + rim
voice b = r.displace(1/16) + clap
```

Displace by a beat to start a riff in a new place. Here notes fill the moved rhythm.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 g1 bb1].on([x . x . . x . .].displace(1/4)).inst(bass)
voice kick = [kick . . .]*2
```

Displacement inside [`every`](#every) gives a rhythm that stumbles once in a while.

```tine
voice perc = [x . x x . x . .].every(4, r => r.displace(1/8)) + rim
```

See also: [rotate](#rotate), [late](#late), [mutate](#mutate).

### flip

`flip(p)`: Hits become rests and rests become hits, on the rhythm's grid.

`flip` turns hits into rests and rests into hits, on the rhythm's own grid. It gives the answer to a rhythm: the part that fills its gaps.

A kick pattern and its flip on the hats make a complete, interlocking beat.

```tine
let k = [x . . x . . x .]
voice kick = k + kick
voice hats = k.flip + hat
```

Call and response: one line plays the rhythm, the other plays in its gaps.

```tine
let r = [x x . x . . x .]
voice call  = [c4 e4 g4 e4].on(r).inst(pluck)
voice reply = [g4 a4 b4 a4].on(r.flip).inst(bell).vel(.5)
```

Flipping a rhythm with only a few hits gives a busy one, so it suits a quiet ghost part.

```tine
let back = [. . . . x . . . . . . . x . . .]
voice snare = back + snare
voice ghost = back.flip.thin(6) + snare.vel(.25)
```

See also: [minus](#minus), [union](#union), [rhythm](#rhythm).

### thin

`thin(p, n: 1)`: Remove n hits from each loop of a rhythm, never the downbeat (seeded).

`thin(n)` removes n hits from each loop of a rhythm. It never removes the downbeat, and which hits go is seeded, so a thinned rhythm replays the same way.

Sixteenth hats with four hits taken out of each bar.

```tine
voice hats = [x*16].thin(4) + hat
```

Thin a busy melody's rhythm to give it room. The notes still play in order.

```tine
voice lead = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^5 ^6 ^5 ^3 ^2].on([x*8].thin(3)).inst(pluck)
```

A rhythm that thins more as the bars go by, using a different amount each bar.

```tine
voice perc = per_bar(n => [x*8].thin(n % 4 * 2)) + rim
```

See also: [fill](#fill), [degrade](#degrade), [minus](#minus).

### fill

`fill(p, n: 1)`: Add n hits on empty steps of each loop of a rhythm (seeded).

`fill(n)` adds n hits on empty steps of each loop of a rhythm. Which steps get filled is seeded. It is the opposite of [`thin`](#thin).

A sparse kick with one extra hit added somewhere in each bar.

```tine
voice kick = [x . . . x . . .].fill(1) + kick
```

Fill a rhythm only on the last bar of four, for a busier turnaround.

```tine
voice snare = [. . x . . . x .].every(4, r => r.fill(3)) + snare
```

Fill and thin together keep the count of hits the same but change where they are.

```tine
voice lead = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^6].on([x . x . x . x .].thin(1).fill(1)).inst(pluck)
```

See also: [thin](#thin), [union](#union), [mutate](#mutate).

### union

`union(a, b)`: Every hit of either rhythm (one hit where both have one).

`union(a, b)` is every hit of either rhythm. Where both have a hit, there is one hit.

Two simple rhythms combined into a more interesting one.

```tine
let tres = [x . . x . . x .]
let even = [x . x . x . x .]
voice both = union(tres, even) + rim
```

Union of two Euclidean rhythms is a common way to build a clave or a bell pattern.

```tine
voice bell = union(x.euclid(3, 8), x.euclid(2, 8, rot: 1)) + cowbell
```

Use the union as a rhythm for notes: the melody plays wherever either part did.

```tine
let low  = [x . . . x . . .]
let high = [. . x . . . x x]
voice tune = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^3 ^2].on(union(low, high)).inst(pluck)
```

See also: [intersect](#intersect), [minus](#minus), [stack](#stack).

### intersect

`intersect(a, b)`: The hits of a that b also has.

`intersect(a, b)` keeps the hits of a that b also has. It finds where two rhythms agree.

Accent the places where a three-beat and a four-beat pattern meet.

```tine
let threes = [x . . x . . x . . x . . x . . .]
let fours  = [x . . . x . . . x . . . x . . .]
voice a = threes + rim
voice b = intersect(threes, fours) + crash
```

A bass that plays only where both the kick and a syncopated rhythm do.

```tine
let four = [x . . x . . x . x . . x . . x .]
let push = [x . x x . x x . x . x x . x x .]
voice low  = [c2 eb2 g1].on(intersect(four, push)).inst(bass)
voice drum = four + kick
```

Intersect with a rotated copy of itself to keep only the hits that repeat a step apart.

```tine
let r = [x x . x x x . x]
voice a = intersect(r, r.rotate(1)) + hat
```

See also: [union](#union), [minus](#minus).

### minus

`minus(a, b)`: The hits of a that b does not have.

`minus(a, b)` keeps the hits of a that b does not have. It carves one rhythm out of another.

Steady eighths with the snare's hits taken out, so the hats leave space for the snare.

```tine
let back = [. . x . . . x .]
voice snare = back + snare
voice hats  = minus([x*8], back) + hat
```

A melody that answers the bass, playing only where the bass does not.

```tine
let under = [x . . x . . x .]
voice low  = [c2 g1 bb1].on(under).inst(bass)
voice high = [e4 g4 a4 c5].on(minus([x*8], under)).inst(bell).vel(.5)
```

Subtract a thinned copy to get the hits the thinning removed.

```tine
let r = [x*8]
voice kept = r.thin(3) + hat
voice gone = minus(r, r.thin(3)) + rim
```

See also: [flip](#flip), [intersect](#intersect), [union](#union).

### mutate

`mutate(p, rate: 0.1)`: Each loop, about rate of the hits move one step left or right, and stay moved: the rhythm wanders. Seeded and replayable, counted from the section's start.

`mutate(rate)` lets a rhythm wander. Each loop, about `rate` of its hits move one step left or right, and they stay moved. Like all randomness in Tine it is seeded and counted from the section's start, so the wandering replays exactly.

A clave that slowly drifts away from where it started.

```tine
seed 4
voice clave = [x . . x . . x . . . x . x . . .].mutate(.15) + clave
```

The original next to a mutating copy, so you can hear the two pull apart.

```tine
seed 9
let r = [x . x . . x . x]
voice home = r + rim
voice away = r.mutate(.25) + cowbell
```

Mutate the rhythm a melody rides on. The notes keep their order; only their timing wanders.

```tine
seed 2
voice lead = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^4 ^3 ^2].on([X . . x . . X . . . x . X . . .].mutate(.1)).inst(pluck)
```

See also: [displace](#displace), [thin](#thin), [evolve](#evolve).

### trunc

`trunc(p, fraction)`: Play only the first fraction of each bar.

`trunc(fraction)` plays only the first part of each bar and leaves the rest silent. It cuts a phrase short without changing its timing.

Keep three quarters of a bar: the last two eighths drop out.

```tine
voice line = [c4 d4 e4 f4 g4 a4 b4 c5].trunc(3/4).inst(pluck)
```

Inside [`every`](#every), trunc leaves a gap for another part, here once every four bars.

```tine
voice drums = [kick hat snare hat kick kick snare hat].every(4, p => p.trunc(1/2))
```

[`per_bar`](#per_bar) can give each bar its own amount, so the phrase gets shorter bar by bar.

```tine
voice tune = per_bar(n => [^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^6 ^7 ^8].trunc(1 - (n % 4) / 4)).inst(keys)
```

See also: [degrade](#degrade), [loop](#loop).

### per_bar

`per_bar(bar => pattern)`: Build each bar from a function of the bar number. Randomness inside is keyed to the bar.

`per_bar` builds each bar from a function of the bar number (from 0). Anything computed inside, including randomness, is decided per bar and stays the same each time that bar plays.

Transpose a riff up a step each bar, over four bars.

```tine
voice riff = per_bar(n => [c3 eb3 g3 eb3].transpose((n % 4) * 2)).inst(bass)
```

`if` inside the function picks a different pattern on certain bars.

```tine
voice drums = per_bar(n => if n % 4 == 3 then [snare*8] else [kick hat snare hat])
```

Random choices inside are keyed to the bar: each bar picks its own chord, and the same seed picks the same ones.

```tine
seed 7
voice keys = per_bar(n => pick([^1@7 ^4@7 ^6@7 ^2@7])).strum.inst(keys)
```

See also: [evolve](#evolve), [every](#every), [cat](#cat).

### evolve

`evolve(start, (state, bar) => next, (state, bar) => pattern)`: Carry state from bar to bar. Bar 0 plays view(start); each later bar's state is step(previous state, bar). Replayable: states are always computed forward from bar 0.

`evolve(start, step, view)` carries a value from bar to bar. Bar 0 plays `view(start)`, and each later bar steps the value forward. Because it is always computed from bar 0, any bar can be jumped to and sounds the same.

A counter. The state is a number that goes up by one each bar, and the view plays it as a scale degree.

```tine
voice climb = evolve(0, (n, bar) => (n + 1) % 8, (n, bar) => [n n n n].degrees).inst(pluck)
```

A random walk in pitch: each bar moves the note by a small random step, and the view builds a figure on it.

```tine
seed 3
voice walk = evolve(c4, (p, bar) => p + pick([-2 -1 1 2]), (p, bar) => [p (p + 7) (p + 12) (p + 7)]).inst(keys)
```

Without a view, the state itself plays. Here the state is a whole phrase, and each bar rotates it by one.

```tine
voice turn = evolve([c4 d4 e4 g4], (p, bar) => p.rotate(1)).inst(bell)
```

See also: [per_bar](#per_bar), [mutate](#mutate), [voicelead](#voicelead).

### loop

`loop(p, bars)`: Repeat the first `bars` bars of p forever.

`loop(bars)` repeats the first few bars of a pattern forever. It freezes something that would otherwise change, like a random line or a long form.

A random melody changes every bar. Looping its first two bars turns it into a riff you can keep.

```tine
seed 12
voice riff = dice([^1 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^7 .], 8).loop(2).inst(pluck)
```

Loop the opening of a longer pattern to hear just that part.

```tine
voice keys = [c4@maj a3@m f3@maj g3@maj].slow(4).loop(1).inst(keys)
```

Loop works on [`per_bar`](#per_bar) too, so a generated part can be pinned down to its first bars.

```tine
voice bass = per_bar(n => [c2 . c2 g1].transpose(n * 5)).loop(3).inst(bass)
```

See also: [slow](#slow), [per_bar](#per_bar), [trunc](#trunc).

## Chance

### humanize

`humanize(p, time: 0.004, vel: 0.1)`: Seeded random drift in timing (bars) and velocity. Replayable like all randomness.

`humanize` nudges each note's timing and velocity by a small random amount, so a part sounds played rather than programmed. Like all randomness here it is seeded: the same seed gives the same feel.

The defaults: a few milliseconds of timing drift and a little velocity spread.

```tine
seed 5
voice keys = [c4@maj7 . . c4@maj7 . . a3@m7 .].humanize.inst(keys)
```

More velocity spread and less timing drift suits hi-hats, where the dynamics matter most.

```tine
seed 5
voice hats = [hat*16].humanize(time: .002, vel: .25)
voice beat = [kick . snare .]
```

A loose, late-night feel: more timing drift, together with swing.

```tine
seed 5
voice ride = [ride*8].swing.humanize(time: .01, vel: .15)
voice bass = [c2 e2 g2 bb2].inst(upright).humanize(time: .01)
```

See also: [swing](#swing), [degrade](#degrade).

### degrade

`degrade(p, amount: 0.5)`: Randomly drop events (seeded).

`degrade` drops events at random. The amount is the chance each one is dropped, 0.5 by default. The amount can be a signal, so a part can thin out and fill in over time.

Half the sixteenth hats removed: a sparse, shifting pattern.

```tine
seed 2
voice hats = [hat*16].degrade
voice beat = [kick . snare .]
```

A small amount just takes the odd note out of a line, which keeps a loop from feeling mechanical.

```tine
seed 2
voice arp = [c4 e4 g4 b4 c5 b4 g4 e4].fast(2).degrade(.15).inst(pluck)
```

A signal for the amount: here a slow [`drift`](#drift) makes the part breathe in and out over several bars.

```tine
seed 2
voice texture = [hat*16].degrade(drift(.25)).vel(.5)
```

See also: [thin](#thin), [sometimes](#sometimes), [maybe](#maybe).

### sometimes

`sometimes(p, prob, f)`: Apply f to each event with the given probability (seeded).

`sometimes(prob, f)` applies f to each event with the given chance. Leave out the chance and it is one in two. [`often`](#often) and [`rarely`](#rarely) are shortcuts for 75% and 25%.

Some notes jump up an octave.

```tine
seed 8
voice arp = [c4 e4 g4 c5 g4 e4 c4 e4].sometimes(p => p.octave(1)).inst(pluck)
```

A low chance for an occasional ornament: a few hats become a quick double hit.

```tine
seed 8
voice hats = [hat*8].sometimes(.2, p => p.ply(2))
voice beat = [kick . snare .]
```

The change can be anything, including sound settings. Some notes ring out with reverb.

```tine
seed 8
voice bell = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^8].inst(bell).sometimes(.3, p => p.reverb(.8).vel(.4))
```

See also: [often](#often), [rarely](#rarely), [maybe](#maybe), [degrade](#degrade).

### often

`often(p, f)`: Apply f to about 75% of events.

`often(f)` applies f to about three events in four. It is [`sometimes(.75, f)`](#sometimes).

Most notes are short; a few are left long, which gives an accent by contrast.

```tine
seed 3
voice bass = [c2 c2 eb2 c2 g1 c2 bb1 c2].often(p => p.legato(.3)).inst(bass)
```

Most hats are soft, so the few loud ones stand out.

```tine
seed 3
voice hats = [hat*16].often(p => p.vel(.3))
```

See also: [sometimes](#sometimes), [rarely](#rarely).

### rarely

`rarely(p, f)`: Apply f to about 25% of events.

`rarely(f)` applies f to about one event in four. It is [`sometimes(.25, f)`](#sometimes), for surprises that should stay surprising.

Now and then a note slides down a step of the scale.

```tine
seed 6
voice tune = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^3 ^4 ^2 ^5 ^1].rarely(p => p.step(-1)).inst(pluck)
```

An occasional open hat among the closed ones.

```tine
seed 6
voice hats = [hat*8].rarely(p => p.map(h => ohat))
voice kick = [kick . . kick . . kick .]
```

See also: [sometimes](#sometimes), [often](#often).

### maybe

`maybe(p, prob, f)`: Apply f to whole bars with the given probability (seeded).

`maybe(prob, f)` decides once per bar whether to apply f to the whole bar. Where [`sometimes`](#sometimes) changes notes here and there, `maybe` changes whole bars, which suits fills and variations.

About one bar in three the drums double up.

```tine
seed 11
voice drums = [kick hat snare hat].maybe(.33, p => p.fast(2))
```

Some bars of the melody are played backwards.

```tine
seed 11
voice tune = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^5 ^6 ^5 ^3 ^2].maybe(.5, rev).inst(keys)
```

See also: [every](#every), [sometimes](#sometimes).

### dice

`dice(list, steps: 1)`: A new seeded random pick from list on each of `steps` steps per bar.

`dice(list, steps)` picks a new random element from a list on each step. It is the quickest way to an endless melody that stays inside a set of notes. Put rests in the list to leave space.

Eight random picks per bar from a pentatonic set.

```tine
seed 21
voice tune = dice([^1 ^2 ^3 ^5 ^6], 8).inst(pluck)
```

Rests in the list make silence part of the choice. More rests, more space.

```tine
seed 21
voice spark = dice([^5 ^8 ^9 ^10 . . .], 16).inst(bell).vel(.35)
```

Lists can hold anything a phrase can, including whole sub-patterns, so the dice picks beats, not just notes.

```tine
seed 21
voice drums = dice([[kick hat] [snare hat] [kick kick] [hat hat]], 4)
```

See also: [walk](#walk), [pick](#pick), [scramble](#scramble).

### walk

`walk(list, steps: 8, stride: 1)`: A seeded random walk through list: each step moves at most `stride` places.

`walk(list, steps, stride)` takes a random walk through a list: each step moves at most `stride` places from the last. Lines move by small steps, so they sound sung rather than scattered.

A walk through a scale, eight steps per bar, one step at a time.

```tine
seed 4
voice tune = walk([^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^6 ^7 ^8], 8).inst(keys)
```

A larger stride lets the line leap now and then.

```tine
seed 4
voice tune = walk([c4 d4 e4 g4 a4 c5 d5 e5], 8, stride: 3).inst(pluck)
```

Walk through numbers and turn them into scale steps with [`degrees`](#degrees).

```tine
seed 4
key d dorian
voice line = walk(0..10, 8).degrees.inst(bell).vel(.5)
```

See also: [dice](#dice), [evolve](#evolve).

### scramble

`scramble(p)`: Shuffle the elements of a phrase into a new seeded order each bar.

`scramble` shuffles the elements of a phrase into a new order each bar. The notes are always the same ones, so the harmony holds while the line changes.

A four-note chord shape in a new order every bar.

```tine
seed 9
voice arp = [c4 e4 g4 b4].scramble.fast(2).inst(pluck)
```

Scramble a drum bar: the same hits, rearranged.

```tine
seed 9
voice drums = [kick hat snare hat kick kick snare hat].scramble
```

Inside [`every`](#every), the line is scrambled only once in a while.

```tine
seed 9
voice tune = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^5 ^6 ^5 ^3 ^2].every(4, p => p.scramble).inst(keys)
```

See also: [shuffle](#shuffle), [dice](#dice).

### rand

`rand()`: A seeded random number in [0, 1). Same seed, same number.

`rand()` is a random number from 0 up to 1. It is decided when the code runs, once per call, so use it to set up a piece. Inside [`per_bar`](#per_bar) or [`map`](#map) it is decided per bar or per note.

A random tempo between 90 and 110, fixed by the seed.

```tine
seed 30
tempo 90 + floor(rand() * 20)
voice beat = [kick hat snare hat]
```

Inside [`per_bar`](#per_bar), it is decided again for each bar. Here each bar gets its own loudness.

```tine
seed 30
voice hats = per_bar(n => [hat*8].vel(.3 + rand() * .6))
```

Print it to see the number the seed gives.

```tine
seed 30
print(rand(), rand())
voice tone = [c4]
```

See also: [rand_int](#rand_int), [noise](#noise), [chance](#chance).

### rand_int

`rand_int(lo, hi)`: A seeded random whole number from lo to hi inclusive.

`rand_int(lo, hi)` is a random whole number from lo to hi, both included.

Choose a transposition for the whole piece.

```tine
seed 12
let shift = rand_int(-3, 3)
voice tune = [c4 e4 g4 e4].transpose(shift).inst(pluck)
```

Inside [`per_bar`](#per_bar), each bar picks its own number. Here it is how many times each note repeats.

```tine
seed 12
voice hats = per_bar(n => [hat hat hat hat].ply(rand_int(1, 3)))
```

Random octave jumps on a bass line, decided bar by bar.

```tine
seed 12
voice bass = per_bar(n => [c2 . c2 g1].octave(rand_int(0, 1))).inst(bass)
```

See also: [rand](#rand), [pick](#pick).

### pick

`pick(list)`: One seeded random element of list.

`pick(list)` is one random element of a list. Like [`rand`](#rand), it is decided when the code runs, or per bar inside [`per_bar`](#per_bar).

Pick an instrument for the piece.

```tine
seed 14
voice tune = [c4 e4 g4 c5].inst(pick([pluck bell keys]))
```

Inside [`per_bar`](#per_bar), a new chord each bar from a small set.

```tine
seed 14
voice keys = per_bar(n => pick([^1@7 ^4@9 ^6@7 ^2@7])).strum.inst(keys)
```

Pick a whole pattern: each bar gets one of three drum grooves.

```tine
seed 14
voice drums = per_bar(n => pick([[kick hat snare hat] [kick kick snare .] [kick . snare snare]]))
```

See also: [weighted](#weighted), [dice](#dice), [rand](#rand).

### weighted

`weighted(list, weights)`: A seeded random element, chosen in proportion to weights.

`weighted(list, weights)` picks one element, with each chosen in proportion to its weight. Use it when some choices should be common and others rare.

The tonic chord most of the time, the others less often.

```tine
seed 16
voice keys = per_bar(n => weighted([^1@7 ^4@7 ^5@7], [5 2 1])).strum.inst(keys)
```

Mostly quarter notes, sometimes eighths, rarely a triplet.

```tine
seed 16
voice hats = per_bar(n => weighted([[hat*4] [hat*8] [hat*12]], [6 3 1]))
```

See also: [pick](#pick), [dice](#dice).

### shuffle

`shuffle(list)`: The list in a seeded random order (decided once).

`shuffle(list)` puts a list in a random order, decided once. Where [`scramble`](#scramble) reshuffles every bar, `shuffle` gives one fixed order, so it makes a riff.

A scale in a random order makes a riff. Change the seed for another.

```tine
seed 18
voice riff = shuffle([^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^6 ^7 ^8]).inst(pluck)
```

Shuffle a drum bar once and keep it.

```tine
seed 18
voice drums = shuffle([kick kick snare hat hat hat . .])
```

See also: [scramble](#scramble), [pick](#pick).

### chance

`chance(prob)`: true with the given probability (seeded).

`chance(prob)` is true with the given probability. Use it with `if` to decide between two things.

Decide once whether the piece has a bass line.

```tine
seed 20
voice beat = [kick hat snare hat]
voice bass = if chance(.5) then [c2 . c2 g1].inst(bass) else [c3 . . .].inst(bass)
```

Inside [`per_bar`](#per_bar), each bar decides for itself: here, whether to play a fill.

```tine
seed 20
voice drums = per_bar(n => if chance(.3) then [snare*8] else [kick hat snare hat])
```

See also: [maybe](#maybe), [rand](#rand).

## Pitch

### transpose

`transpose(p, semitones)`: Move by semitones (fractions allowed: 0.5 is a quarter tone). Works on notes, degrees, chords and patterns.

`transpose(n)` moves notes by n semitones. It works on notes, degrees, chords and whole patterns, and n can be a fraction for microtones. Writing `p + n` does the same.

A riff and the same riff a fifth higher, alternating bars.

```tine
let riff = [c3 eb3 g3 eb3]
voice bass = cat(riff, riff.transpose(7)).inst(bass)
```

A pattern of amounts moves the line around under a fixed rhythm: a whole progression from one figure.

```tine
voice arp = [c4 e4 g4 e4].fast(2).transpose(<0 5 7 0>).inst(pluck)
```

Half a semitone is a quarter tone. Here a copy a quarter tone up makes a beating, out-of-tune chorus.

```tine
voice a = [c4 e4 g4 c5].inst(organ).pan(-.6)
voice b = [c4 e4 g4 c5].transpose(.5).inst(organ).pan(.6).vel(.4)
```

See also: [octave](#octave), [step](#step), [within](#within).

### octave

`octave(p, n)`: Move by n octaves (of the scale's period for degrees).

`octave(n)` moves notes by whole octaves. On scale degrees it moves by the scale's period, which matters in tunings where the octave is not 12 semitones.

Write a bass line in the middle register and drop it two octaves.

```tine
key d dorian
voice bass = [^1 . ^1 ^5 . ^4 _ .].octave(-2).inst(bass)
```

Double a melody an octave up, quieter, for a brighter tone.

```tine
let tune = [e4 g4 a4 _ g4 e4 d4 .]
voice lead = tune.inst(pluck)
voice high = tune.octave(1).inst(bell).vel(.3)
```

A pattern of octaves makes the line jump between registers.

```tine
voice bounce = [c3 c3 c3 c3].octave([0 1 0 2]).inst(pluck)
```

See also: [transpose](#transpose), [within](#within).

### step

`step(p, n)`: Move by n steps of the current scale (diatonic transposition).

`step(n)` moves notes by n steps of the current scale. It is diatonic transposition: up a step in C major, E goes to F but C goes to D. That keeps a line in key, which [`transpose`](#transpose) does not.

A line and its copy two steps up, a third apart all the way, always in key.

```tine
key c major
let tune = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^4 ^3 ^2]
voice lead = tune.inst(keys)
voice third = tune.step(2).inst(keys).vel(.5)
```

A sequence: the same figure moved down a step each bar.

```tine
key a minor
voice seq = [^5 ^4 ^5 ^3].step(<0 -1 -2 -3>).inst(pluck)
```

It works on note names too, reading them in the key.

```tine
key g major
voice line = [g4 a4 b4 d5].step(1).inst(bell)
```

See also: [transpose](#transpose), [degrees](#degrees), [key](#key).

### degrees

`degrees(p)`: Treat numbers as 0-based scale steps: [0 2 4].degrees is [^1 ^3 ^5].

`degrees` reads numbers as scale steps counted from 0, so `[0 2 4]` becomes `[^1 ^3 ^5]`. It joins number-crunching (counters, walks, maps) to the key.

A counting pattern played in the current key.

```tine
key d dorian
voice scale = [0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7].degrees.inst(pluck)
```

Arithmetic on numbers first, then degrees: the scale in thirds.

```tine
key e minor
voice thirds = run(8).map(i => i * 2).degrees.inst(keys)
```

A random walk through numbers, then degrees, stays in key and moves by step.

```tine
seed 4
key f lydian
voice line = walk(0..9, 8).degrees.inst(bell)
```

See also: [run](#run), [step](#step), [key](#key).

### key

`key(root, scale) or p.key(root, scale)`: Make a key, or play p in a key. Degrees like ^3 resolve against it.

`key(root, scale)` makes a key. As a method, `p.key(root, scale)` plays p in that key, so the same degrees can sound in different keys in different parts. The `key` statement sets the key for the whole piece.

The same degrees in two keys at once: polytonality.

```tine
let tune = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^3 ^4 ^2 ^7 ^1]
voice upper = tune.key(c4, major).inst(keys)
voice lower = tune.key(f#3, major).inst(keys).vel(.5)
```

Change mode under a fixed line. The degrees stay the same; the notes change.

```tine
let tune = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^5 ^6 ^5 ^3 ^2]
voice line = cat(tune.key(d4, dorian), tune.key(d4, phrygian), tune.key(d4, lydian), tune.key(d4, mixolydian)).inst(pluck)
```

A key with a scale built from a tuning. Here a 7-note scale from 31 equal steps.

```tine
voice line = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^6 ^7 ^8].key(c4, edo(31, [0 5 10 13 18 23 28])).inst(bell)
```

See also: [degrees](#degrees), [step](#step), [mode](#mode), [scale](#scale).

### chord

`chord(root, quality)`: A chord: chord(c4, "maj7") is the same as c4@maj7. With one text argument it reads a chord symbol: chord("Bb7#11").

`chord(root, quality)` builds a chord, the same as `root@quality`. With a single text argument it reads a chord symbol, which is handy when the symbol comes from text.

A chord from a root and a quality.

```tine
voice pad = chord(c3, "maj9").inst(pad)
```

Read a symbol straight from text, slash bass and all.

```tine
voice keys = cat(chord("Bb7#11"), chord("Ebmaj7/G")).strum.inst(keys)
```

Inside [`map`](#map), build a chord on every note of a line.

```tine
voice stabs = [c4 . f4 . g4 . c4 .].map(n => chord(n, "m7")).legato(.3).inst(keys)
```

See also: [changes](#changes), [invert](#invert), [tones](#tones).

### invert

`invert(p, n: 1)`: Chord inversion: move the lowest n notes up an octave.

`invert(n)` moves the lowest n notes of each chord up an octave. Inversions keep the harmony but change its color and make smoother movement between chords.

A C major chord in root position, then first and second inversion.

```tine
voice keys = cat(c4@maj, c4@maj.invert(1), c4@maj.invert(2)).inst(keys)
```

Invert chords in a progression so they move less.

```tine
voice keys = [c4@maj f4@maj.invert(2) g4@maj.invert(1) c4@maj].inst(keys)
```

A negative number goes the other way: the top note drops an octave.

```tine
voice pad = c4@maj7.invert(-1).inst(pad)
```

See also: [voicelead](#voicelead), [drop2](#drop2), [within](#within).

### arp

`arp(p, mode: "up")`: Spread each chord's notes across its length. Modes: up, down, updown, downup, out, random.

`arp(mode)` spreads each chord's notes across its length, one after another. Modes are `up`, `down`, `updown`, `downup`, `out` (outside in) and `random`.

A chord progression, arpeggiated up.

```tine
voice arp = <c4@maj7 a3@m7 d4@m7 g3@7>.arp.inst(pluck)
```

`updown` goes up and back down without repeating the top note, and [`fast`](#fast) fits two in a bar.

```tine
voice arp = <c4@m9 ab3@maj7>.arp("updown").fast(2).inst(keys)
```

Each chord's arpeggio fills its own step, so chords of different lengths give different speeds.

```tine
voice arp = [c4@maj7:3 g3@7].arp("down").inst(bell)
```

`random` picks a new seeded order for every chord.

```tine
seed 3
voice arp = [c4@m7 c4@m7 f4@m7 g4@7].arp("random").inst(pluck)
```

See also: [strum](#strum), [tones](#tones), [held](#held).

### strum

`strum(p, spread: 1/48)`: Roll each chord's notes, low to high, `spread` bars apart.

`strum(spread)` rolls each chord's notes from low to high, a small time apart, like a guitar strum. The spread is in bars; the default 1/48 is quick.

A progression, gently strummed.

```tine
voice keys = <^1@7 ^4@7 ^5@7 ^1@7>.strum.inst(keys)
```

A slower spread sounds like a harp.

```tine
voice harp = [c4@maj9 . . . f4@maj9 . . .].strum(1/16).inst(pluck)
```

A pattern of chords played on the beat, strummed, for rhythm guitar.

```tine
voice gtr = [e3@m _ e3@m e3@m . e3@m . .].strum(1/64).inst(pluck)
```

See also: [arp](#arp).

### hz

`hz(pitch)`: Frequency of a pitch in Hz (at the current tuning).

`hz(pitch)` is a pitch's frequency in Hz, at the current tuning. Use it to set an effect's frequency from a note, or just to look.

Print the frequency of A4, and of middle C.

```tine
print(hz(a4), hz(c4))
voice tone = [a4]
```

Tune a ring modulator to a note, so its metallic tone fits the harmony.

```tine
voice bell = [c4 e4 g4 c5].inst(sine).ring(hz(g5), mix: .6)
```

See also: [note_num](#note_num), [pitch](#pitch).

### note_num

`note_num(pitch)`: The (possibly fractional) MIDI note number of a pitch.

`note_num(pitch)` is a pitch's MIDI note number. It can be fractional, for microtones. Use it for arithmetic on pitches.

Print a few note numbers.

```tine
print(note_num(c4), note_num(a4), note_num(c4 + 50c))
voice tone = [c4]
```

Use the note number for arithmetic. Here every note is mirrored around E4 (note 64), turning the line upside down.

```tine
voice line = [c4 d4 e4 g4 a4 g4].inst(keys)
voice flip = [c4 d4 e4 g4 a4 g4].map(n => pitch(128 - note_num(n))).octave(-1).inst(bass)
```

See also: [pitch](#pitch), [hz](#hz).

### pitch

`pitch(n)`: A pitch from a MIDI note number (fractions allowed).

`pitch(n)` turns a MIDI note number into a pitch. Fractions are allowed. It is the way back from arithmetic to notes.

Compute notes from numbers: a harmonic-ish series of MIDI numbers.

```tine
voice tones = [0 12 19 24 28 31].map(k => pitch(36 + k)).inst(sine).vel(.4)
```

Fractional numbers give microtones: 24 equal steps per octave.

```tine
voice quarter = run(8).map(i => pitch(60 + i / 2)).inst(bell)
```

See also: [note_num](#note_num), [hz](#hz).

### ratio

`ratio(r)`: The size of a frequency ratio in semitones: ratio(3/2) is about 7.02.

`ratio(r)` is the size of a frequency ratio in semitones: `ratio(3/2)` is about 7.02, a pure fifth. Use it to tune intervals by ratio instead of by semitone.

Compare an equal-tempered fifth with a pure one.

```tine
print(ratio(3/2), ratio(5/4))
voice tone = [c4]
```

A pure major third above a note, played against the equal-tempered one: listen to the beating.

```tine
voice pure  = [c4 . (c4 + ratio(5/4)) .].inst(sine)
voice equal = [. c4 . e4].inst(sine)
```

See also: [just](#just), [transpose](#transpose).

### scale

`scale(semitones, period: 12)`: A scale from semitone offsets (fractions allowed).

`scale(steps)` makes a scale from semitone offsets. Fractions are allowed, and `period:` sets the interval it repeats at (12 by default). Use it with [`key`](#key) to play degrees in it.

A pentatonic scale written out, then used for a line.

```tine
key c scale([0 2 4 7 9])
voice line = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^6 ^5 ^3].inst(pluck)
```

Fractional steps: a scale with a neutral third, between minor and major.

```tine
key d scale([0 2 3.5 5 7 8.5 10])
voice line = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^4 ^3 ^2].inst(bell)
```

A scale that repeats at a twelfth (19 semitones) instead of the octave, like the Bohlen-Pierce idea.

```tine
key c3 scale([0 3 5 8 11 14 16], period: 19)
voice line = run(8).degrees.inst(keys)
```

See also: [just](#just), [edo](#edo), [cents](#cents), [mode](#mode).

### just

`just(ratios, period: 2)`: A just-intonation scale from frequency ratios, e.g. just([1 9/8 5/4 3/2 5/3]).

`just(ratios)` makes a just-intonation scale from frequency ratios. Its intervals are pure, without the slight beating of equal temperament.

A just major scale: chords on it ring very still.

```tine
key c3 just([1 9/8 5/4 4/3 3/2 5/3 15/8])
voice chords = <^1@3 ^4@3 ^5@3 ^1@3>.inst(organ)
```

A scale from the harmonic series, with the seventh and eleventh harmonics.

```tine
key d just([1 9/8 5/4 11/8 3/2 13/8 7/4])
voice line = walk(0..10, 8).degrees.inst(bell)
voice drone = {d2 a2}.inst(pad)
```

See also: [ratio](#ratio), [scale](#scale), [cents](#cents).

### edo

`edo(n, steps)`: An n-tone equal division of the octave. With steps, a scale picked from it: edo(31, [0 5 10 13 18 23 28]).

`edo(n)` divides the octave into n equal steps. With a list of steps it picks a scale from them. 31 steps per octave, for instance, gives thirds close to pure.

A diatonic scale picked from 31 equal steps, close to quarter-comma meantone.

```tine
key c edo(31, [0 5 10 13 18 23 28])
voice chords = <^1@7 ^4@7 ^5@7 ^1@3>.strum(1/24).inst(organ)
```

All 24 steps of quarter-tone tuning, played as a slow climb.

```tine
key c4 edo(24)
voice climb = run(24).degrees.inst(bell)
```

A five-note scale from 5 equal steps per octave: no step is a familiar interval.

```tine
key c4 edo(5)
voice line = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^4 ^3 ^2].inst(pluck)
```

See also: [scale](#scale), [cents](#cents), [just](#just).

### cents

`cents(list, period: 1200)`: A scale from offsets in cents.

`cents(list)` makes a scale from offsets in cents, where 100 cents is a semitone. Many published tunings are written in cents.

A gamelan-like pelog scale.

```tine
key e cents([0 120 270 540 670 785 950])
voice gongs = [^1 . . . ^5 . ^4 .].octave(-1).inst(bell)
voice saron = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^5 ^3 ^2 ^1 ^7].inst(pluck)
```

A scale of equal 150-cent steps that repeats at the octave.

```tine
key c4 cents([0 150 300 450 600 750 900 1050])
voice line = run(8).degrees.inst(keys)
```

See also: [scale](#scale), [scala](#scala).

### scala

`scala(text)`: A scale from the text of a Scala .scl file (the common microtonal tuning format).

`scala(text)` reads a scale from the text of a Scala `.scl` file, the common format for microtonal tunings. Lines starting with `!` are comments; then a name, a count, and one interval per line in cents or as a ratio. In a string, `\n` starts a new line.

A pelog tuning written as text, with a line break written as `\n`.

```tine
let pelog = scala("! pelog\nPelog, approximate\n7\n120.0\n270.0\n540.0\n670.0\n785.0\n950.0\n2/1")
key e pelog
voice line = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^5 ^6 ^5 ^3 ^2].inst(bell)
```

Ratios work too. This is a just pentatonic scale.

```tine
key c4 scala("just pentatonic\n5\n9/8\n5/4\n3/2\n5/3\n2/1")
voice line = run(6).degrees.inst(pluck)
```

See also: [scala_file](#scala_file), [cents](#cents).

### scala_file

`scala_file(path)`: A scale loaded from a Scala .scl file next to your piece.

`scala_file(path)` loads a scale from a Scala `.scl` file next to your piece. It needs the file, so it works from the command line and in a DAW opened on a file, but not in a page with no files.

Load a tuning from a file and play in it. (This one needs `pelog.scl` beside the piece.) *(Needs a file, a device or the network to be heard.)*

```tine device
key e scala_file("pelog.scl")
voice line = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^5 ^6 ^5 ^3 ^2].inst(bell)
```

Keep the scale in a name and use it in several keys. *(Needs a file, a device or the network to be heard.)*

```tine device
let pelog = scala_file("pelog.scl")
voice high = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^3].key(e4, pelog).inst(bell)
voice low  = [^1 . ^5 .].key(e2, pelog).inst(bass)
```

See also: [scala](#scala).

### mode

`mode(scale, n)`: Rotate a scale to start on its n-th degree (1-based): mode(major, 2) is dorian.

`mode(scale, n)` rotates a scale to start on its n-th degree, counting from 1. `mode(major, 2)` is dorian; it works on any scale, including custom and microtonal ones.

The modes of the major scale, one per bar, over the same degrees.

```tine
let up = [^1 ^2 ^3 ^4 ^5 ^6 ^7 ^8]
voice line = cat(up.key(d4, mode(major, 1)), up.key(d4, mode(major, 2)), up.key(d4, mode(major, 3)), up.key(d4, mode(major, 4))).inst(pluck)
```

A mode of a custom scale: start a pentatonic on its third note.

```tine
key c mode(scale([0 2 4 7 9]), 3)
voice line = run(6).degrees.inst(bell)
```

See also: [scale](#scale), [key](#key).

### within

`within(p, lo, hi: lo + 12)`: Move each note or chord by whole octaves until it sits in lo..hi (a chord moves by its lowest note and keeps its shape). changes(...).bassnote.within(e1, e2) folds a bass line into one octave.

`within(lo, hi)` moves each note or chord by whole octaves until it sits between lo and hi. A chord moves by its lowest note and keeps its shape. It keeps generated parts in a playable range.

Fold a bass line taken from chord changes into one octave, so it does not jump around.

```tine
voice bass = changes("Dm7 G7 | Cmaj7 A7").bassnote.within(e1, e2).inst(bass)
```

Keep a random melody in a singable range.

```tine
seed 5
voice tune = dice([c3 e4 g5 a2 d6 f4], 8).within(c4, c5).inst(keys)
```

Chords keep their shape while they are moved into place.

```tine
voice keys = [c5@maj7 f2@maj7 g6@7 a3@m7].within(c4).inst(keys)
```

See also: [octave](#octave), [root](#root), [bassnote](#bassnote).

## Sound

### vel

`vel(p, v)`: Velocity 0 to 1. v may itself be a pattern: .vel([1 .5 .7 .5]).

`vel(v)` sets how hard notes are played, from 0 to 1. The value can be a pattern, which is how accents are written, or a signal, for swells and fades.

One level for a whole part, to sit it back in the mix.

```tine
voice pad  = <c3@maj7 a2@m7>.inst(pad).vel(.4)
voice lead = [e4 g4 a4 b4].inst(pluck)
```

A pattern of velocities accents the hats. It repeats across the notes on its own grid.

```tine
voice hats = [hat*8].vel([.9 .4 .6 .4])
```

A signal for a crescendo over two bars.

```tine
voice roll = [snare*16].vel(saw(2).range(.1, 1))
```

See also: [gain](#gain), [humanize](#humanize).

### legato

`legato(p, x)`: Note length as a fraction of its step (1 = full, 0.5 = staccato).

`legato(x)` sets how long each note sounds, as a fraction of its step. 1 is full length, 0.5 is staccato, more than 1 overlaps the next note.

Short, plucked chords.

```tine
voice stabs = [c4@m7 . c4@m7 . . c4@m7 . .].legato(.3).inst(keys)
```

A pattern of lengths gives articulation: long, short, short, long.

```tine
voice line = [c4 d4 e4 g4].legato([1 .3 .3 1]).inst(organ)
```

More than 1 makes notes overlap, smooth like a pad.

```tine
voice wash = [c4 e4 g4 b4].legato(2).inst(pad).vel(.4)
```

See also: [dur](#dur), [slur](#slur), [release](#release).

### gain

`gain(p, x)`: Output level multiplier for the built-in synth.

`gain(x)` multiplies the built-in synth's output level. Unlike [`vel`](#vel), it does not change how a note is played (the attack, the brightness), only how loud it comes out.

Turn a part down without softening its attack.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 . c2 g1].inst(bass).gain(.5)
voice kick = [kick . kick .]
```

Above 1 to boost a quiet instrument.

```tine
voice tune = [e5 d5 c5 g4].inst(sine).gain(1.5)
```

See also: [vel](#vel), [compress](#compress).

### pan

`pan(p, x)`: Stereo position from -1 (left) to 1 (right).

`pan(x)` places a part in the stereo field, from -1 (left) through 0 (centre) to 1 (right). Patterns and signals move it.

Two guitars, one each side.

```tine
voice left  = [e3@m . e3@m e3@m].strum.inst(pluck).pan(-.7)
voice right = [. b3@m . b3@m].strum.inst(pluck).pan(.7)
```

A pattern pans each note in turn: a ping-pong.

```tine
voice ping = [c5 e5 g5 c6].pan([-1 1]).inst(bell)
```

A slow signal makes the part drift across.

```tine
voice drift = [^1 ^3 ^5 ^3].inst(keys).pan(sine(4).range(-.8, .8))
```

See also: [drift](#drift), [sine](#sine).

### cutoff

`cutoff(p, hz)`: Filter cutoff for the built-in synth.

`cutoff(hz)` sets the built-in synth's low-pass filter for each note. Lower is darker. With [`res`](#res) and a moving signal, it is the classic filter sweep. For a filter over the whole voice's mix, use [`lpf`](#lpf).

A dark bass and a bright one.

```tine
voice dark   = [c2 . c2 .].inst(saw).cutoff(300).pan(-.6)
voice bright = [. g2 . g2].inst(saw).cutoff(4000).pan(.6)
```

A pattern of cutoffs, one per note, for a squelchy line.

```tine
voice acid = [a1 a1 a2 a1 c2 a1 g2 a1].inst(saw).cutoff([300 800 2000 500]).res(.7)
```

A slow sine sweep over eight bars.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 c2 c3 c2 eb2 c2 g2 bb1].fast(2).inst(saw).cutoff(sine(8).range(300, 3000)).res(.4)
```

See also: [res](#res), [fenv](#fenv), [lpf](#lpf), [wobble](#wobble).

### res

`res(p, x)`: Filter resonance 0 to 1.

`res(x)` sets the resonance of the synth's filter, 0 to 1. Higher values make the filter whistle at the cutoff, which makes sweeps more vocal.

Low and high resonance on the same line.

```tine
voice smooth = [c2 c3 c2 eb2].inst(saw).cutoff(800).res(.1)
voice sharp  = [c2 c3 c2 eb2].inst(saw).cutoff(800).res(.8).late(1/2)
```

High resonance with a sweeping cutoff: the acid sound.

```tine
voice acid = [a1 a1 a2 a1 c2 a1 g2 a1].fast(2).inst(saw).cutoff(tri(2).range(300, 2500)).res(.75)
```

See also: [cutoff](#cutoff), [fenv](#fenv).

### attack

`attack(p, seconds)`: Envelope attack time.

`attack(seconds)` sets how long a note takes to reach full volume. Short is percussive; long swells in.

A slow attack turns a keyboard into a swelling pad.

```tine
voice swell = <c3@maj7 f3@maj7>.inst(keys).attack(.8)
```

A pattern of attacks: some notes snap, some fade in.

```tine
voice line = [c4 e4 g4 c5].inst(saw).attack([.005 .2]).cutoff(1500)
```

See also: [decay](#decay), [sustain](#sustain), [release](#release).

### release

`release(p, seconds)`: Envelope release time.

`release(seconds)` sets how long a note takes to fade after it ends. Long releases blur notes together.

Short notes with a long release ring on after they stop.

```tine
voice bells = [c5 . g4 . e5 . . .].legato(.2).inst(sine).release(1.5)
```

A tight release for a dry, clipped sound.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 c2 . c2 eb2 . g1 .].inst(saw).release(.02).cutoff(900)
```

See also: [attack](#attack), [legato](#legato).

### decay

`decay(p, seconds)`: Envelope decay time.

`decay(seconds)` sets how long a note takes to fall from its peak to the sustain level.

A fast decay to a low sustain gives a plucked sound.

```tine
voice pluck = [c4 e4 g4 c5].inst(saw).decay(.1).sustain(.1).cutoff(2500)
```

A long decay lets each note fade slowly while held.

```tine
voice keys = <c3@maj7 a2@m7>.inst(saw).decay(2).sustain(0).cutoff(1200)
```

See also: [sustain](#sustain), [attack](#attack).

### sustain

`sustain(p, level)`: Envelope sustain level 0 to 1.

`sustain(level)` sets the level a held note settles to after its decay, 0 to 1.

Full sustain holds like an organ; zero sustain dies away like a struck string.

```tine
voice organ  = [c4@maj . . .].inst(saw).sustain(1).cutoff(1500).pan(-.6)
voice struck = [. . c4@maj .].inst(saw).sustain(0).decay(.4).cutoff(1500).pan(.6)
```

A pattern of sustain levels makes each note's body different.

```tine
voice line = [c3 _ eb3 _ g3 _ bb3 _].inst(saw).decay(.2).sustain([.8 .1]).cutoff(1200)
```

See also: [decay](#decay), [release](#release).

### reverb

`reverb(p, amount)`: Send to the built-in reverb, 0 to 1.

`reverb(amount)` sends a part to the shared reverb, 0 to 1. All voices share one room, so they sound as if they are in the same place. For a reverb on one voice alone, use [`room`](#room).

A dry drum part and a wet melody.

```tine
voice drums = [kick hat snare hat]
voice tune  = [e5 . d5 . c5 . g4 .].inst(bell).reverb(.6)
```

Patterned sends: every other note goes into the room.

```tine
voice keys = [c4 e4 g4 c5].inst(keys).reverb([0 .8])
```

See also: [room](#room), [delay](#delay).

### hpf

`hpf(p, hz)`: High-pass filter on the whole voice: removes rumble below hz. Unlike cutoff, which shapes each note, this filters the voice's mix.

`hpf(hz)` is a high-pass filter on the whole voice: it removes everything below hz. Use it to keep low rumble out of parts that do not need it.

Thin out a pad so it does not crowd the bass.

```tine
voice pad  = <c3@m9 f3@m9>.inst(pad).hpf(500)
voice bass = [c2 . c2 g1].inst(bass)
```

A rising high-pass, the build-up before a drop.

```tine
voice beat = [kick hat snare hat]*2
voice keys = [c4@m7 . . c4@m7].inst(keys).hpf(saw(4).range(100, 3000))
```

See also: [lpf](#lpf), [cutoff](#cutoff).

### lpf

`lpf(p, hz)`: Low-pass filter on the whole voice: darkens everything above hz. Try .lpf(sine(8).range(400, 3400)) for a sweep.

`lpf(hz)` is a low-pass filter on the whole voice: it darkens everything above hz. Unlike [`cutoff`](#cutoff), which shapes each note in the synth, this filters the voice's mix, so it works on samples and chords alike.

A sweep on a drum loop.

```tine
voice amen = ["loop_amen"].loopAt(2).chop(16).lpf(sine(4).range(400, 6000))
```

Muffle a part to push it into the background.

```tine
voice back = [c4@maj7 . a3@m7 .].inst(keys).lpf(800)
voice lead = [e5 d5 c5 b4].inst(pluck)
```

See also: [hpf](#hpf), [cutoff](#cutoff).

### drive

`drive(p, amount)`: Saturation on the whole voice, 0 (clean) to 1 (crushed). Chords distort together, like an amp.

`drive(amount)` saturates the whole voice, from 0 (clean) to 1 (crushed). Chords distort together, like through an amp.

A little drive warms a bass.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 . c2 eb2 . f2 g2 .].inst(bass).drive(.3)
```

A lot of drive on power chords.

```tine
voice gtr = [e2@5 _ e2@5 g2@5 _ a2@5 _ .].inst(saw).drive(.9).lpf(3000)
```

See also: [crush](#crush), [compress](#compress).

### delay

`delay(p, mix, time: 3/16, feedback: .4)`: An echo on the whole voice. mix 0 to 1; time in bars (3/16 is a dotted eighth in 4/4); feedback 0 to .95 sets how many repeats.

`delay(mix, time, feedback)` is an echo on the whole voice. Time is in bars, so it follows the tempo: 3/16 is a dotted eighth in 4/4. Feedback sets how many repeats. For echoes as separate notes, use [`echo`](#echo).

A dotted-eighth delay on a sparse melody.

```tine
voice tune = [e5 . . g5 . . a5 .].inst(pluck).delay(.4)
```

A quarter-note delay with long feedback, for dub.

```tine
voice chop = [. c4@m . .].inst(keys).legato(.2).delay(.5, time: 1/4, feedback: .7)
```

A tiny time with feedback makes a metallic, flanged sound.

```tine
voice zap = [c3 . c3 .].inst(saw).delay(.6, time: 1/256, feedback: .8)
```

See also: [echo](#echo), [room](#room).

### wave

`wave(p, name)`: Oscillator of the synth instrument (and its presets): saw, square, pulse, tri, sine, super, fm or noise.

`wave(name)` picks the oscillator of the `synth` instrument and its presets: saw, square, pulse, tri, sine, super, fm or noise.

The same line on four waves, one per bar.

```tine
let line = [c3 eb3 g3 bb3]
voice synth = cat(line.inst(synth).wave("saw"), line.inst(synth).wave("square"), line.inst(synth).wave("tri"), line.inst(synth).wave("sine"))
```

`super` is a stack of detuned saws, the trance lead.

```tine
voice lead = [e4 . g4 a4 . b4 a4 g4].inst(synth).wave("super").unison(7).detune(20)
```

See also: [inst](#inst), [pw](#pw), [unison](#unison).

### pw

`pw(p, width)`: Pulse width of the pulse wave, 0 to 1 (.5 is square). May be a pattern or a signal.

`pw(width)` sets the width of the pulse wave, 0 to 1. 0.5 is a square; narrow widths sound thin and nasal. Move it with a signal for pulse-width modulation.

A narrow pulse for a reedy tone.

```tine
voice reed = [c4 d4 e4 g4].inst(synth).wave("pulse").pw(.15)
```

Slow pulse-width modulation: the classic analog string sound.

```tine
voice strings = <c3@maj7 f3@maj7>.inst(synth).wave("pulse").pw(sine(2).range(.1, .5)).attack(.3)
```

See also: [wave](#wave).

### detune

`detune(p, cents)`: Spread of the unison voices, in cents either side.

`detune(cents)` spreads the unison oscillators apart, in cents either side. More detune is wider and more chorused.

Slight and heavy detune, side by side.

```tine
voice slight = [c3@maj7].inst(synth).wave("saw").unison(5).detune(5).pan(-.6)
voice heavy  = [. . c3@maj7 .].inst(synth).wave("saw").unison(5).detune(40).pan(.6)
```

Detune moving over time, for a sound that widens.

```tine
voice lead = [e4 _ g4 _ a4 _ b4 _].inst(supersaw).detune(saw(2).range(0, 50))
```

See also: [unison](#unison), [chorus](#chorus).

### unison

`unison(p, n)`: How many detuned oscillators sound together (1 to 16).

`unison(n)` sets how many detuned oscillators sound together, from 1 to 16. More is thicker.

One oscillator, then sixteen.

```tine
voice one  = [c3 . . .].inst(synth).wave("saw").unison(1)
voice many = [. . c3 .].inst(synth).wave("saw").unison(16).detune(25)
```

A thick bass from three oscillators and a sub.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 . c2 eb2].inst(synth).wave("saw").unison(3).detune(10).sub(.5).cutoff(900)
```

See also: [detune](#detune), [sub](#sub).

### sub

`sub(p, level)`: A sine one octave below, 0 to 1.

`sub(level)` adds a sine one octave below, 0 to 1. It gives weight to a bass without muddying it.

A bass with and without a sub.

```tine
voice plain = [c2 . . .].inst(synth).wave("square").cutoff(800)
voice deep  = [. . c2 .].inst(synth).wave("square").cutoff(800).sub(.8)
```

Sub on a reese bass.

```tine
voice reese = [c2 _ _ _ eb2 _ _ _].inst(reese).sub(.6)
```

See also: [unison](#unison), [octave](#octave).

### glide

`glide(p, seconds)`: Slide into each note from the one before it in the voice. On a note slurred into (c4~ d4), the slide joins the two into one sound.

`glide(seconds)` slides into each note from the one before it in the voice. A pattern of glide times slides only on some notes, the way an acid bass line does.

Every note glides a little: a portamento lead.

```tine
voice lead = [c4 e4 g4 e4 a4 g4 e4 d4].inst(saw).glide(.08).cutoff(2000)
```

Glide on only one note in eight.

```tine
voice acid = [a1 a1 a2 a1 c2 a1 g2 a1].inst(tb303).glide([0 0 .06 0])
```

Slurred into, the glide joins two notes into one sound.

```tine
voice slide = [c4~ g4 . e4~ c4 .].inst(saw).glide(.15).cutoff(1800)
```

See also: [slur](#slur), [gliss](#gliss).

### slur

`slur(p)`: Play p's notes as one connected sound, without a new attack on each, up to the last note in each bar. Scores draw a slur. For one pair, write c4~ d4 in the phrase.

`slur` plays a phrase's notes as one connected sound, without a new attack on each, up to the last note in each bar. Scores draw a slur over them. For one pair of notes, write `c4~ d4` in the phrase.

A whole bar slurred: one breath.

```tine
voice tune = [c4 d4 e4 g4 a4 g4 e4 d4].slur.inst(saw).cutoff(1800)
```

Slur against detached notes, for contrast.

```tine
voice phrase = cat([e4 f4 g4 a4].slur, [e4 f4 g4 a4].legato(.3)).inst(strings)
```

Slur plus glide slides through every note.

```tine
voice siren = [c4 g4 c5 g4].slur.glide(.2).inst(sine)
```

See also: [glide](#glide), [gliss](#gliss), [legato](#legato).

### gliss

`gliss(p, amount: 1)`: Glissando: each note slides to the next across the last `amount` of its length (1 = all of it), up to the last note in each bar. amount may be a pattern: .gliss([1 0]).

`gliss(amount)` makes each note slide to the next across the last part of its length (1 = all of it), up to the last note in each bar. The amount can be a pattern, to slide only some notes.

A full glissando between every note.

```tine
voice slide = [c4 g4 e4 c5].gliss.inst(sine)
```

Slide only on the second half of each note: the pitch holds, then bends.

```tine
voice bend = [c4 e4 g4 a4].gliss(.5).inst(strings)
```

A pattern of amounts: slide, hold, slide, hold.

```tine
voice line = [c4 d4 e4 f4 g4 f4 e4 d4].gliss([1 0]).inst(saw).cutoff(1500)
```

See also: [glide](#glide), [slur](#slur), [vibrato](#vibrato).

### fenv

`fenv(p, octaves, attack: .001, decay: .2)`: Filter envelope: the cutoff jumps up by this many octaves and falls back over decay seconds. The acid squelch.

`fenv(octaves, attack, decay)` is a filter envelope: on each note, the cutoff jumps up by this many octaves and falls back over the decay. It is the squelch of acid bass.

A plucky bass from a filter envelope.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 . c2 eb2 . g2 c2 .].inst(saw).cutoff(300).fenv(3)
```

A pattern of amounts gives each note its own squelch.

```tine
voice acid = [a1 a1 a2 a1 c2 a1 g2 a1].inst(tb303).fenv([4 2 3 1])
```

A slow decay makes a sweep inside each long note.

```tine
voice pad = <c3@m9 ab2@maj9>.inst(saw).cutoff(400).fenv(3, decay: 1.5)
```

See also: [cutoff](#cutoff), [res](#res), [wobble](#wobble).

### fm

`fm(p, index, ratio: 2, decay: .4)`: Frequency modulation (switches the synth to the fm wave): index is brightness, ratio the modulator's pitch, decay how fast the brightness fades.

`fm(index, ratio, decay)` adds frequency modulation and switches the synth to its FM wave. Index is brightness, ratio is the modulator's pitch against the note, decay is how fast the brightness fades. Whole-number ratios sound harmonic; others sound like bells and metal.

An electric-piano tone from a low index and a ratio of 1.

```tine
voice ep = [c4@maj7 . . a3@m7].fm(2, ratio: 1).inst(fm)
```

A bell from an inharmonic ratio.

```tine
voice bell = [c5 . g5 . e5 . . .].fm(5, ratio: 3.5, decay: 1)
```

A pattern of indices: the line gets brighter and darker.

```tine
voice bass = [c2 c2 c3 c2].fm([1 4 8 2], ratio: 2, decay: .2)
```

See also: [wave](#wave), [ring](#ring).

### vibrato

`vibrato(p, rate: 5, depth: .3)`: Pitch wobble, rate in Hz, depth in semitones.

`vibrato(rate, depth)` wobbles the pitch. Rate is in Hz, depth in semitones.

A gentle singer's vibrato.

```tine
voice lead = [e4 _ _ g4 a4 _ _ .].inst(strings).vibrato(5, depth: .15)
```

Deep and slow, for a wobbly, seasick sound.

```tine
voice wob = [c4@maj7].inst(organ).vibrato(1.5, depth: .5)
```

See also: [gliss](#gliss), [wobble](#wobble).

### wobble

`wobble(p, rate: 2, depth: 2)`: Filter wobble in time with the music: rate in cycles per bar, depth in octaves.

`wobble(rate, depth)` swings the synth's filter in time with the music. Rate is in cycles per bar; depth is in octaves. Patterns of rates give the dubstep wub.

A wobble bass, two wubs per bar.

```tine
voice wub = [a0 _ _ _ c1 _ _ _].inst(wobble).wobble(2, depth: 4)
```

A pattern of rates: the wub speeds up halfway.

```tine
voice wub = [a0 _ _ _ c1 _ _ _].inst(wobble).wobble([2 4], depth: 4)
```

A slow wobble on a pad, one sweep per bar.

```tine
voice pad = <c3@m7 f3@m7>.inst(saw).wobble(1, depth: 2).vel(.5)
```

See also: [cutoff](#cutoff), [fenv](#fenv).

### vowel

`vowel(p, v)`: Formant filter: makes the voice say a vowel, "a" "e" "i" "o" or "u". v may be a pattern: .vowel(["a" "o"]).

`vowel(v)` is a formant filter that makes the voice say a vowel: "a", "e", "i", "o" or "u". It works on any sound. A pattern of vowels makes it talk.

A saw bass that says "o".

```tine
voice bass = [c2 c2 eb2 c2].inst(saw).vowel("o")
```

A pattern of vowels, one per note.

```tine
voice talk = [c3 c3 c3 c3 eb3 c3 g3 c3].inst(saw).vowel(["a" "e" "i" "o"])
```

Vowels on drums.

```tine
voice beat = [kick hat snare hat].vowel(["a" "u"])
```

See also: [lpf](#lpf), [phaser](#phaser).

### crush

`crush(p, bits)`: Bit crusher: fewer bits (1 to 16) is rougher. .crush(4) is very lo-fi.

`crush(bits)` is a bit crusher: fewer bits (from 16 down to 1) is rougher. 4 is very lo-fi.

A crushed drum loop.

```tine
voice beat = [kick hat snare hat kick kick snare hat].crush(4)
```

A pattern of bit depths: the crunch comes and goes.

```tine
voice keys = [c4@m7 . c4@m7 .].inst(keys).crush([16 3])
```

See also: [coarse](#coarse), [drive](#drive).

### coarse

`coarse(p, n)`: Sample-rate reduction: holds every nth sample, for aliasing and grit. 1 is off.

`coarse(n)` reduces the sample rate by holding every nth sample. It adds aliasing and grit. 1 is off.

A gritty, aliased lead.

```tine
voice lead = [e4 g4 a4 b4].inst(square).coarse(8)
```

With [`crush`](#crush), the full 8-bit sound.

```tine
voice chip = [c5 e5 g5 c6].fast(2).inst(chip).coarse(4).crush(6)
```

See also: [crush](#crush).

### ring

`ring(p, hz, mix: 1)`: Ring modulation: multiplies the voice by a sine at hz, for metallic and bell-like tones.

`ring(hz, mix)` ring-modulates the voice by a sine at hz, for metallic and bell-like tones. Low frequencies make a tremolo instead.

A sine line turned into bells.

```tine
voice bells = [c4 e4 g4 c5].inst(sine).ring(830)
```

A low frequency sounds like tremolo.

```tine
voice trem = [c4@maj7].inst(organ).ring(6, mix: .5)
```

A pattern of frequencies for a robot voice.

```tine
voice robot = [c3*8].inst(saw).ring([200 300 450 300])
```

See also: [fm](#fm), [hz](#hz).

### chorus

`chorus(p, mix: .5, rate: .8, depth: .5)`: Chorus: thickens the voice with slightly detuned, moving copies. rate in Hz.

`chorus(mix, rate, depth)` thickens the voice with slightly detuned copies that move. Rate is in Hz.

A chorused electric piano.

```tine
voice keys = <c4@maj7 a3@m7>.inst(keys).chorus(.6)
```

Fast and deep, for a seasick shimmer.

```tine
voice gtr = [e4 b4 g4 b4].inst(pluck).chorus(.8, rate: 4, depth: .9)
```

See also: [phaser](#phaser), [detune](#detune).

### phaser

`phaser(p, mix: .5, rate: .5, depth: .7)`: Phaser: a sweeping notch, the classic swirl. rate in Hz.

`phaser(mix, rate, depth)` sweeps a notch through the sound: the classic swirl. Rate is in Hz.

A phased pad.

```tine
voice pad = <c3@m9 f3@m9>.inst(pad).phaser(.6, rate: .25)
```

Phaser on a talking acid line.

```tine
voice acid = ([c2 c2 c3 c2 eb2 c2 g2 bb1]*2).inst(saw).vowel(["a" "o"]).phaser(.5)
```

See also: [chorus](#chorus), [vowel](#vowel).

### compress

`compress(p, threshold: -18, ratio: 4)`: Compressor on the whole voice: levels above threshold (dB) are reduced by ratio, then made up. Evens out a part.

`compress(threshold, ratio)` evens out a voice: levels above the threshold (in dB) are reduced by the ratio, then the whole is made up. Loud and soft notes end up closer together.

Even out a part with widely varied velocities.

```tine
voice keys = [c4 e4 g4 c5].vel([1 .2 .9 .3]).inst(keys).compress(-24, ratio: 6)
```

Heavy compression on drums for punch.

```tine
voice beat = [kick hat snare hat].compress(-30, ratio: 8)
```

See also: [gain](#gain), [duck](#duck).

### room

`room(p, mix: .3, size: .5)`: A reverb on this voice alone, unlike reverb(), which sends to the shared room. size 0 to 1.

`room(mix, size)` is a reverb on this voice alone. [`reverb`](#reverb) sends to a room all voices share; `room` gives one part its own space.

A small room on the snare, a large one on the pad.

```tine
voice snare = [. snare . snare].room(.4, size: .2)
voice pad   = <c3 eb3>.inst(pad).room(.5, size: .9)
```

A pattern of mixes: every other note is wet.

```tine
voice clap = [clap*4].room([0 .8], size: .7)
```

See also: [reverb](#reverb), [delay](#delay).

### duck

`duck(p, voice, depth: .8, release: 1/8)`: Sidechain-style ducking: this voice dips each time the named voice plays a note, then recovers over release bars. .duck("kick") pumps a pad against the kick.

`duck(voice)` makes this voice dip each time the named voice plays, then recover over the release (in bars). It is sidechain compression: the pad pumps against the kick.

A pad that ducks under the kick.

```tine
voice kick = [kick . . . kick . . .]
voice pad  = <c3@m7 ab2@maj7>.inst(pad).duck("kick")
```

Deeper and slower, for an obvious pump.

```tine
voice kick = [kick*4]
voice bass = [c2*8].inst(saw).cutoff(900).duck("kick", depth: 1, release: 1/4)
```

See also: [compress](#compress).

### dur

`dur(p, beats)`: Fixed note length in beats, independent of the step length.

`dur(beats)` sets each note's length in beats, whatever its step. A note can ring past its step, or be cut short, without changing the rhythm.
